newsitem.title: USA: MCI holders okay merger with British Telecom.
newsitem.headline: MCI holders okay merger with British Telecom.

text.p: MCI Communications Corp., holding probably its final annual meeting Wednesday in the hometown of the company's founder, won shareholder approval of a $23 billion merger with British Telecommunications Plc.
MCI stockholders cast more than 77 percent of outstanding shares in favour of the trans-Atlantic deal.

The merger, if approved by British Telecom shareholders and national regulators, would create a combined company known as Concert Plc, with $40.6 billion in revenues and an eye on caputuring telecommunications markets worldwide.

"That same MCI competitive spirit that revolutionised the U.S. communications industry will be the driving force as part of the new Concert in opening markets worldwide to the delight of millions of users," MCI Chairman Bert Roberts told shareholders.

The meeting was held at King's College in this northeastern Pennsylvania town, home of the late William McGowan, who co-founded MCI 30 years ago and led its successful challenge to the telephone monopoly held by AT&T Corp.

MCI is now the second largest U.S. long-distance company. After the merger, the combined firm would be the second largest telecommunications company in the world, with about 6 percent of the $670 billion global telecommunications market.
"We are going to go after the remaining 94 percent," Roberts said.

The merger awaits regulatory approvals in Washington, London and Brussels, the headquarters of the European Union. British Telecom shareholders are scheduled to vote on the merger at an extraordinary general meeting April 15.
In an interview, Roberts said he was encouraged by the pace of the regulatory process.

Asked if the approval process was on track to be completed before the fall, Roberts said, "We're hoping." But he added the company has continued to officially target a fall completion for the deal announced last November.
MCI expected to receive indications from the European Union in about two weeks on how it will rule on the merger, Roberts said. A formal ruling is due by June 11.

Roberts also said "we haven't found what I would call any major difficulties, or any difficulties" with the U.S. Justice Department regrding its approval process, which is expected to lead to a decision in late May or June.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission also must approve the deal along with the Defence Department, which has authority over certain security-related issues. Roberts said the FCC would probably act 30 to 60 days after the Justice Department.
Roberts also said MCI would continue its drive to capture local telephone markets in the United States, where MCI now expects to serve 25 markets by the end of the second quarter.
Although MCI has not been as aggressive as long-distance rivals AT&T or Sprint Corp. in offering local service, Roberts said MCI's initial consumer acceptance has been strong.
"The growth rates are very good," he said in the interview. "They're very small numbers compared to the whole, but we're very excited about it."

He said the key to success in the local access business would be a favourable ruling May 8 from the Federal Communications Commission on the level of access charges that can be assessed by regional Bell operating companies.

Concert's initial focus, Roberts said, would probably be in expanding existing areas of British Telecom's and MCI's cooperation since 1994, in expanding global internet services, especially to business, and in expanding a network of alliances with telecommunications firms around the world.
MCI and British Telecom together carry close to half the world's internet traffic, he said.
